title: Wildcard Matching
directAnswer: Match string s against a pattern p where '?' matches any single character and '*' matches any sequence (including empty). It's a 2-D grid DP: dp[i][j] is true if the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p. A normal char or '?' aligns one-to-one (dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]); a '*' either consumes one more character of s (dp[i-1][j]) or matches the empty string (dp[i][j-1]). O(n·m) time and space, reducible to O(m). The trap is the empty-prefix base case: a leading run of '*' must still match an empty s.

remember.pattern: 2-D grid DP over (prefix of s, prefix of p); '*' branches into match-one vs match-empty
remember.formula:
dp[0][0] = true
dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-1] if p[j-1]=='*'   (stars match empty)
if p[j-1]=='?' or p[j-1]==s[i-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]
elif p[j-1]=='*':                  dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] OR dp[i][j-1]
else:                              dp[i][j] = false
answer = dp[n][m]
rules: `'*'` has **two** moves: match one more character of `s` (`dp[i-1][j]`, star stays) or match the empty string and move past it (`dp[i][j-1]`).
`'?'` and a literal match consume **exactly one** character each from `s` and `p`: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`.
Base case `dp[i][0] = false` for `i > 0` (empty pattern can't match non-empty s), but `dp[0][j]` can be **true** if `p[0..j)` is all stars.
Don't confuse this with regex matching: here `'*'` stands alone (any sequence), it is **not** 'zero or more of the previous character'.
The whole DP is monotone in one direction, so you can compress to a single rolling row → O(m) space.
whenToUse: Match a string against a pattern with single-char and multi-char wildcards
Two-sequence alignment where one side has 'match-any' tokens
Any problem reducible to 'does prefix of A align with prefix of B' with flexible tokens
antiSignals: '*' means 'zero or more of the preceding element' → that's Regular Expression Matching, a different transition
You need the actual alignment, not just yes/no → reconstruct from the table, still DP
Pattern has no wildcards → plain string equality, no DP needed
You want all matching substrings in a text → Aho–Corasick / suffix automaton, not this DP
remember.takeaway: Wildcard Matching is the canonical two-prefix grid DP. The only subtlety is the '*' branch — match-one (consume a char, star stays) OR match-empty (skip the star) — and the empty-string base case where a leading run of stars must still match. Get those right and it's the same dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] alignment skeleton as Edit Distance and LCS.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model it as a 2-D prefix-vs-prefix DP, get the two-way '*' transition right (match one more char OR match empty), and handle the empty-s base case where leading stars still match.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Treating '*' like regex '*' (zero-or-more of the previous char), botching the dp[0][j] base row so leading stars don't match an empty string, or forgetting that '*' can match the empty sequence.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the recurrence cleanly: literal/'?' aligns one-to-one, '*' is dp[i-1][j] OR dp[i][j-1]. Nail the base row, then mention the O(m) rolling-array compression and contrast '*' here vs regex '*'.

problemStatement:
Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p`, implement wildcard matching that supports:

- `'?'` — matches any **single** character.
- `'*'` — matches any sequence of characters, **including the empty sequence**.

The match must cover the ***entire*** input string `s` (not a partial match). Return `true` if `p` matches `s`, otherwise `false`.

Here `s` contains only lowercase letters; `p` contains lowercase letters, `'?'`, and `'*'`.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
'*' matches any sequence including empty; '?' matches exactly one character
understanding: Ask whether the first i characters of s can be produced by the first j characters of p. Each pattern character is one of three kinds: a literal (must equal the current s char), '?' (matches any single char), or '*' (a flexible token that can absorb zero or more characters of s). The answer to the whole problem is whether all of s is consumed by all of p, i.e. dp[n][m]. The only branching comes from '*', which can either grab another character of s or step aside as the empty match.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does '*' mean 'any sequence' or 'zero or more of the previous character'?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any sequence (glob-style), including empty. It's NOT the regex meaning. That changes the '*' transition entirely — here '*' stands on its own.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can '*' match the empty string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A pattern like '*' matches '' and 'abc' alike. That's why dp[i][j-1] (star matches empty) is part of the transition and why a leading run of stars must match an empty s.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the pattern cover all of s?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — it's a full match, not a search. The answer is dp[n][m], requiring all of s consumed by all of p.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if s is empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then p matches only if p is empty or consists entirely of stars. That's exactly what the dp[0][j] base row encodes.

examples.explanation: 'a' matches only the first character; there's no token to consume the second 'a'.
First '*' matches empty, 'a' matches 'a', second '*' matches 'dce', 'b' matches 'b'.
'a' matches 'a', '*' can match 'cd', 'c' matches 'c', '?' matches 'b' — but then there's nothing left to match the final 'b'.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. Two-prefix matching with a multi-char wildcard lands on the grid DP.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursion with Star Branching
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to establish the per-character cases and the two-way '*' branch, then flag the exponential blow-up from stars.
hints: Walk both strings with pointers i (into s) and j (into p). If the pattern char is a literal or '?', it must consume exactly one character of s. When does that succeed?
When you hit a '*', it has two choices: match the empty string and move past it (advance j), or match one more character of s (advance i, keep the '*'). Try both.
Base cases: if you run out of pattern, you match only if s is also exhausted; if you run out of s, the rest of the pattern must be all stars.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each '*' forks into two recursive calls and those forks overlap heavily, so without caching the tree is exponential in n + m. Recursion depth is O(n + m).
approaches.explanation:
Define `solve(i, j)` = does `s[i:]` match `p[j:]`? Handle the pattern character at `j`:

- If `j` reached the end of `p`, the match succeeds only if `i` also reached the end of `s` (nothing left to consume).
- If `p[j]` is `'*'`, branch: either it matches one more character of `s` (recurse `solve(i+1, j)`, the star stays available) or it matches the empty string (recurse `solve(i, j+1)`, step past the star). Return true if either works.
- If `p[j]` is `'?'` or equals `s[i]` (and `i` is in range), it consumes one character on each side: recurse `solve(i+1, j+1)`.
- Otherwise it's a literal mismatch → false.

**The mental shift: '*' is the only source of choice.** Literals and `'?'` are forced moves — they either align one-to-one or fail immediately. All the branching, and all the difficulty, comes from `'*'`, which has to decide *how many* characters of `s` to absorb. Modeling that as 'absorb one more (`i+1`, star stays)' versus 'absorb none (`j+1`)' covers every possibility: repeatedly choosing 'one more' lets a single star swallow any length, and choosing 'none' ends it.

**Why the two base cases.** Running out of pattern with characters of `s` left means failure (nothing to match them). Running out of `s` with pattern left is fine *only* if everything remaining is stars, each matching empty — and the star branch `solve(i, j+1)` naturally walks through exactly that.

**Why we don't ship this.** Each star doubles the recursion, and the same `(i, j)` state is reached through many different star decisions — massive overlap. Caching `solve(i, j)` collapses it to `O(n·m)`.
approaches.insight: The state is the pair of pointers `(i, j)` into the two strings, and the recursion revisits the same `(i, j)` through different star choices. Two-pointer state plus exponential overlap is the textbook signal for an `O(n·m)` two-sequence DP.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization on (i, j)
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once you name the overlap — 'cache solve(i, j) so each pointer pair is computed once'.
hints: solve(i, j) returns the same boolean every call. Where can you store it so each (i, j) is computed once?
Use a 2-D memo of size (n+1) × (m+1) holding a tri-state: unknown / true / false. Check on entry, fill before returning.
There are O(n·m) states and each does O(1) work → O(n·m) time and space.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are (n+1)·(m+1) distinct (i, j) states; each resolves in O(1) given its sub-results → O(n·m) time. The memo is O(n·m); recursion depth is O(n + m) on top.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the exact recurrence but cache `solve(i, j)`. Use a tri-state memo — unknown, true, or false — because the answer is a boolean and you can't use 'false' to mean 'not yet computed'.

**The mental shift: the answer depends only on the two pointers.** Whatever sequence of star decisions brought you to `(i, j)`, the question 'does `s[i:]` match `p[j:]`?' has a fixed answer. Caching by `(i, j)` removes every duplicate subtree, and since there are only `O(n·m)` pointer pairs and each costs `O(1)` to combine, the total is `O(n·m)`.

**Why the state is two indices.** The match position in `s` and the match position in `p` are independent, and both are needed — same shape as Edit Distance and LCS. The memo is naturally 2-D.

**A language note (Java memo vs Python tabulation).** This recursion nests up to `O(n + m)` deep. With lengths up to 2000, that depth can reach ~4000 — comfortably fine in Java, but it **exceeds Python's default recursion limit of about 1000**. So in Python you'd either raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` or, better, switch to the bottom-up table (next approach), which uses no recursion stack at all. This is a concrete case where the same algorithm is cleanest top-down in Java but safest bottom-up in Python.
approaches.insight: Standard DP upgrade: a correct recurrence plus a cache keyed on the true state `(i, j)`, with a tri-state sentinel because the values are booleans. The intellectual work — the two-way star branch — was done in the brute force.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — 2-D Table Over Prefixes (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'dp[i][j] = does the first i chars of s match the first j chars of p', filled row by row.
hints: Let dp[i][j] mean: do the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p? dp[0][0] is true.
Build the base row dp[0][j]: empty s matches a pattern prefix only if it is all stars, so dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-1] when p[j-1]=='*'.
Transition: literal/'?' → dp[i-1][j-1]; '*' → dp[i-1][j] (match one more char) OR dp[i][j-1] (match empty). Answer dp[n][m].
approaches.complexityReasoning: Filling an (n+1)·(m+1) table with O(1) work per cell is O(n·m) time. Each row depends only on the previous, so two rolling rows give O(m) space.
approaches.explanation:
Let `dp[i][j]` be true when the first `i` characters of `s` match the first `j` characters of `p`. Initialise `dp[0][0] = true`, set the base row, then fill the grid row by row. The answer is `dp[n][m]`.

**The base row is where most bugs live.** `dp[0][0] = true` (empty matches empty). For `dp[0][j]` (matching an empty `s` against a pattern prefix), the only way to succeed is if every pattern character so far is a star, each matching the empty string — so `dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-1]` when `p[j-1] == '*'`, and false otherwise. The first column `dp[i][0]` for `i > 0` is false: a non-empty string can't match an empty pattern. Skip the star handling in the base row and patterns like `"*a"` against `"a"` silently fail.

**The transition mirrors the recursion.** For each `i, j ≥ 1`:
- If `p[j-1]` is a literal equal to `s[i-1]`, or `'?'`, the characters align one-to-one: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`.
- If `p[j-1]` is `'*'`, it either matches one more character of `s` (`dp[i-1][j]`, star stays) or matches the empty string (`dp[i][j-1]`, star contributes nothing): `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] || dp[i][j-1]`.
- Otherwise (literal mismatch), `dp[i][j] = false`.

**Why this order works.** `dp[i][j]` reads only cells above (`dp[i-1][*]`) and to the left in the same row (`dp[i][j-1]`). Iterating `i` outer (top to bottom) and `j` inner (left to right) guarantees every dependency is already computed — no recursion, no stack, so the Python recursion-limit problem disappears entirely.

**Space compression.** Since row `i` depends only on row `i-1` and earlier cells of row `i`, keep just two rolling rows (or one row updated carefully) for `O(m)` space.

**Why '*' here ≠ regex '*'.** This `'*'` is a standalone any-sequence token, so its transition combines 'consume a char' and 'consume nothing'. Regex `'*'` means 'zero or more of the *previous* element', which needs a different recurrence looking back at `p[j-2]`. State the contrast — interviewers probe whether you know the difference.
approaches.insight: This is the canonical two-sequence prefix DP: state = (prefix of s, prefix of p), transition = align-one for literal/'?', branch for '*'. The same grid skeleton solves Edit Distance, LCS, and Regular Expression Matching — only the per-cell rule changes. Bottom-up also sidesteps Python's recursion limit.

diagrams.title: Cell dependencies in the prefix grid
diagrams.caption: dp[i][j] reads up-left (align), or for '*' it reads up (match one) and left (match empty). Iterate rows top-down, columns left-right.

edgeCases.behavior: Base row propagates true across all stars → dp[0][m] true.
Only the align-one branch fires — reduces to plain string equality.

pitfalls: Forgetting the base-row star handling — patterns with leading '*' fail against an empty or short s.
Writing the '*' transition as dp[i-1][j-1] — that's the '?'/literal rule; '*' must use up OR left.
Compressing to one row but overwriting dp[i][j-1] before it's read — keep two rows or update carefully.

commonMistakes: Treating '*' as the regex 'zero or more of the previous character' instead of 'any sequence'.
Botching the dp[0][j] base row so a leading run of '*' fails to match an empty string.
Writing the '*' transition like the literal one (dp[i-1][j-1]) and losing the match-empty branch.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Confusing wildcard '*' with regex '*'
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Here '*' stands alone and matches any sequence, so its transition is dp[i-1][j] OR dp[i][j-1]. Regex '*' means 'zero or more of p[j-2]' and needs an entirely different recurrence. Mixing them up produces wrong answers on patterns like "a*".
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
elif pc == '*':
    dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j] or dp[i][j - 1]   # match one more OR match empty

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Base row ignores leading stars
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If dp[0][j] is left false for star prefixes, a pattern like "*a" can never line up its star with an empty s, so "*abc" vs "abc" wrongly fails. Leading stars must match the empty string.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
dp[0][0] = true;
// (nothing else) — dp[0][j] stays false even for stars

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong '*' transition
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Using the align-one rule for '*' forces it to consume exactly one character, so it can neither match empty nor absorb multiple characters. The star must combine 'up' (one more) and 'left' (empty).

followupVariations.hint: A two-pointer greedy that remembers the last '*' position matches in O(n·m) worst case but O(1) space — worth mentioning as a follow-up.

patternNote: Canonical two-sequence prefix DP. Recognise it whenever you ask 'does a prefix of A align with a prefix of B' with flexible match tokens: literals/'?' align one-to-one, '*' branches into match-one (up) OR match-empty (left). Same grid as Edit Distance and LCS; bottom-up also avoids Python's recursion-depth limit on long inputs.
